final_message:
All three versions pass the three samples. Rust is the fast one; `fast.py` is currently slower than `plain.py`, and I stopped at the time budget without fixing that. Rust also has a real correctness gap on very large latencies.

**Algorithm (all three):** one streaming pass. Each line is validated against the SPEC language. Status counts go into 10 buckets, and latencies are stored per path template. Templates are sorted by count, then bytes, and the top 10 get nearest-rank P50/P95/MAX via selection or sort.

**Rust (`rust/src/main.rs`)**
- A hand-written byte parser replaces the regex, so each line is scanned once with no backtracking.
- Reads 1 MiB chunks and carries partial lines over, so memory stays low.
- Template keys go into a `HashMap` with FNV hashing, and the template buffer is reused.
- Percentiles use `select_nth_unstable`, not a full sort.
- Release profile: `opt-level=3`, fat LTO, one codegen unit, `panic=abort`. Single thread, no rayon.
- Limitation: latencies above u64 tenths (about 1.8e18 ms, a 19-digit integer part near the top of range) make it print an error and exit 1. It never prints a wrong number, but it does not meet "correct for any valid input".

**`plain.py`**
- Standard library only. Streams the file line by line with one compiled `fullmatch` regex, which gives the exact SPEC language.
- Template keys are built with a bytes `split`/`join`.
- Output is written as bytes so the line endings stay LF on Windows.

**`fast.py`**
- NumPy, processed in 4 MiB blocks of whole lines.
- The seven field separators are found with `searchsorted`. Each field is then checked on concatenated byte arrays with `reduceat`, so no per-line Python work.
- Template keys are polynomial hashes modulo two primes, computed over the emitted template bytes, with a per-template representative path kept for the output.
- If a latency has more than 18 integer digits, the run falls back to an exact per-line scan of the whole file. This keeps results exact for huge values.
- Current speed is poor: about 19 s on my 2M-line test, versus 9.5 s for `plain.py`. The hot spot is `template_keys`, which runs about 40 full-length NumPy operations per block, including 10 fancy-index gathers for the positional powers. The obvious next step is to hash only the numeric-segment contributions sparsely and drop to one hash, but I have not tried it.

**Measured on a 2M-line, 223 MB file** (the generator put about 13% malformed lines in, not the spec's ~1%, because one path template contained a `.`): Rust 0.73 s, `plain.py` 9.5 s, `fast.py` 19.1 s. All three outputs were byte-identical on this file.

**Testing**
- Samples: all three versions pass s1, s2 and s3.
- Differential fuzz: 24 generated files of 3,000 lines each, with valid lines, targeted mutations (host, method, path, query, status, size, latency, UA, separators, truncation, junk) and missing final newlines, plus 10 edge files (empty, newline only, 19-digit latency, `45ms`, `45.22ms`, empty UA, and so on). The fuzz files were generated with latencies kept within u64 so that Rust could be compared; all matched `plain.py` exactly.
- Test scripts are in `logscan/_work/` (`gen.py`, `run_all.py`, `bench_gen.py`). I deleted the large data files. The folder is not a git repo, so nothing was committed.

request.prompt:
You are writing three versions of the same program, one in Rust and two in Python, for a comparison of how
fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Write these three files:

1. `rust/src/main.rs`: Rust, compiled with rustc 1.99 (edition 2024). The Cargo project in `rust/` is set
   up. The only crates you may use are serde (with derive), serde_json, regex and rayon. They are already
   listed in `rust/Cargo.toml` and vendored, so build offline with `cargo build --release --offline` inside
   `rust/`. Do not add other dependencies. You may change the `[profile.release]` settings in
   `rust/Cargo.toml`.
2. `plain.py`: Python 3.13, standard library only.
3. `fast.py`: Python 3.13, standard library plus NumPy 2.2.

Each program is run with the path of one input file as its argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments). It reads that file and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes. The
Python versions are run as `C:\Python313\python.exe plain.py INPUT_PATH` and
`C:\Python313\python.exe fast.py INPUT_PATH`, and the Rust version as the release binary
`rust/target/release/solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Test all three versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside this
folder, and take at most about 45 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time:
never stop a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example
`taskkill /IM python.exe` or `Stop-Process -Name python`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
